page: Alibaba Cloud ecs.sn1ne.8xlarge is a compute-optimized instance built on the x86_64 architecture. It features 32 dedicated physical cores powered by an Intel Xeon E5-2682v4 processor operating at a base frequency of 2.5 GHz. The instance is equipped with 64.0 GB of system memory, providing a resource density of 2.0 GB per core. It does not include local storage or GPU accelerators, relying on network-attached storage and a baseline network bandwidth of 6 Gbps. Virtualization is managed via the KVM hypervisor.

Benchmark data indicates a clear division between single-core and multi-core capabilities. Single-core performance is consistently weak, falling into the bottom 25% for stress-ng and Geekbench single-core tests, with single-threaded gzip compression scoring in the bottom 10%. However, the 32 dedicated physical cores compensate in parallel workloads. Multi-core CPU performance, Geekbench multi-core, and Passmark CPU scores all rank in the average tier, falling within the middle 50% of tested servers. Similarly, multi-threaded bzip3 decompression and software compilation with Clang achieve average tier results.

Memory performance presents a similar pattern. While the Passmark memory score is weak, memory bandwidth for both small cached blocks and large uncached blocks remains in the average tier. Database operations, Redis SET operations, and static web serving throughput also align with the middle 50% of tested instances. For machine learning workloads, LLM inference using a medium 7B model achieves average prompt processing and text generation speeds, though text generation on smaller models drops to the bottom 25%.

From a qualitative cost-efficiency perspective, the ecs.sn1ne.8xlarge offers a high physical core density on legacy Intel Xeon hardware, making it suitable for multi-threaded workloads that do not require high single-core clock speeds. The lack of bundled local storage means storage costs are externalized to network volumes. This instance is best suited for parallel processing tasks, multi-threaded decompression, software compilation, and moderate database operations where multi-core scaling can offset the lower single-thread performance.
